children: By Suzanne Vranica

OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman once called the combination of ads and artificial intelligence "uniquely unsettling." Now his company is building a sprawling advertising business, at breakneck speed.

It is trying to establish a revenue stream to sustain its free ChatGPT tier and help offset soaring computing costs ahead of its planned initial public offering. In a milestone for the fledgling operation, the company said last month it was on pace to hit $1 billion in annualized ad revenue. But standing up an ad business so quickly has produced mixed results and, some advertisers say, administrative headaches and operational glitches.
OpenAI has taken an "everything, everywhere, all at once" approach to its ad rollout, said NewStreet Research analyst Dan Salmon, calling the pace impressive and unprecedented.

OpenAI started testing ads with some U.S.-based ChatGPT users in February, adding a labeled box featuring a relevant brand below the AI-generated answer. It is introducing tools for advertisers rapidly-to attract Fortune 500 companies but also the small and medium businesses that provide the bulk of ad revenue for Meta Platforms.
"This is one of the fastest ad builds in history, from my experience," said Dave Dugan, OpenAI's head of global ads solutions.

Seven months in, the ad business is now in more than 50 countries. Still, it isn't growing as fast as some industry analysts wanted to see. NewStreet Research recently cut its revenue forecast for the ads business, citing the $1 billion figure.

New ad businesses often experience growing pains. Netflix, which is still growing its ad business, faced early complaints that the subscriber base for its ad tier was too small and advertisers couldn't effectively target specific groups. And advertisers questioned whether Facebook's ad business delivered a good return ahead of its IPO.

Rocket Chief Marketing Officer Jonathan Mildenhall described the performance of his company's OpenAI ads so far as "underwhelming," saying he didn't see any material impact from its testing. Before increasing ad spending, Mildenhall wants better targeting and a smoother transition between chats and ad content.

OpenAI's foray into advertising got off to a bumpy start, initially charging some large brands a steep rate of about $60 per 1,000 views whether or not users clicked. That is a far cry from other digital ad businesses that offer highly targeted ads that brands only pay for when users click through. OpenAI's rates have since fallen significantly, as the company moved to auction-based pricing.

In those early days, it limited how many ads it showed users to monitor whether sponsored content negatively affected the ChatGPT experience. Some brands struggled to spend their allocated budgets because ad opportunities were limited, leading some to pause their participation until the product suite becomes more stable, advertisers said.
"We started with a total focus on user trust," OpenAI's Dugan said, adding that the company is in a different place now that the ad operation has matured.

The company has recruited a string of Meta alums for ad leadership, sales and product engineering roles, including Dugan. It is using its own Codex AI tool to quickly churn out updates and new features.

Three months into the venture, OpenAI introduced its tool that helps track the purchase activity of users who clicked on ads to prove they worked. It took Facebook about a dozen years to do that, Salmon said.
Some brands have been hesitant to deploy the trackers on their sites given the sensitivity around AI and privacy, ad buyers said.
OpenAI's newer ad products are now beginning to resemble some of those offered by Google, Meta and Amazon, including pay-per-click formats and carousels that show multiple products.
It is also experimenting with an ad format that launches a customized ChatGPT conversation when clicked, answering specific questions regarding the advertised product, ad buyers said.

OpenAI introduced a self-serve platform in May that allows companies to upload creative materials, set budgets and track performance-an offering that helps attract small and midsize businesses that can't afford major advertising firms. Ad buyers said the platform wasn't as sophisticated as Google's and Meta's but had still proved effective.
ChatGPT has more than one billion weekly active users, and advertisers say they can't afford to sit on the sidelines as AI changes how people search for information and make buying decisions.
But OpenAI's back-end infrastructure has at times struggled to keep up with demand and some ad executives said the system remains buggy.

Earlier this year, Tamara Rosenthal, the head of marketing at Taskrabbit, was surprised to see thousands of dollars in unfamiliar charges on her company credit card. "I'm being hacked by OpenAI," she recalled telling her accounting department. Her team explained that they had begun testing ads on OpenAI.
Not qualifying for invoicing didn't stop Taskrabbit, which was eager to test the service. "That's how desperate marketers are to get on there," Rosenthal said.
Before expanding its investment, Taskrabbit said it needs better ad-targeting options and more information about how people search on the platform.

Hungryroot CMO Adam Weber said early results were encouraging and he was optimistic about ChatGPT ads because chatbot queries can be more detailed than regular searches, allowing for more personalized ads.

"Even though there's been hiccups, brands can't afford to not test and learn here," said Spencer Lian-Thornton, a vice president at marketing firm Mindgruve. "Ignoring this today is like saying buying stuff online will never catch on."
